rules.title: HIC: Schedule of Progress Payments required (dollars and cents, tied to work)
rules.plain_english: If a home improvement contract calls for any payment other than the downpayment before the job is done, it must include a 'Schedule of Progress Payments' in which every payment is a dollar-and-cents amount tied to a specific phase of work, services or materials. The schedule section must also carry the required bold warning statement.

parameters.trigger: any payment other than the downpayment is due before project completion
parameters.heading: Schedule of Progress Payments
each_payment_must_reference: amount of work or services to be performed
materials and equipment to be supplied
parameters.required_statement_text: The schedule of progress payments must specifically describe each phase of work, including the type and amount of work or services scheduled to be supplied in each phase, along with the amount of each proposed progress payment. IT IS AGAINST THE LAW FOR A CONTRACTOR TO COLLECT PAYMENT FOR WORK NOT YET COMPLETED, OR FOR MATERIALS NOT YET DELIVERED. HOWEVER, A CONTRACTOR MAY REQUIRE A DOWNPAYMENT.
parameters.exempt_if: contractor furnishes bonds/joint control per B&P 7159.5(a)(8)

rules.applies_to: Home improvement contracts (aggregate price over $500) between a contractor and a residential owner or tenant
rules.source_location: PDF page 400 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book; PDF page 410 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book
rules.verbatim_quote: (A) A schedule of progress payments shall be preceded by the heading: “Schedule of Progress Payments.” (B) Each progress payment shall be stated in dollars and cents and specifically reference the amount of work or services to be performed and materials and equipment to be supplied.
rules.notes: This is the HIC equivalent of a schedule of values: a tool can generate it from SOV lines but each line must be a dollar amount tied to described work. B&P 7159.5(a)(4) independently requires the schedule in dollars and cents whenever payments precede completion.

rules.title: HIC: never request or accept payment exceeding work performed or material delivered
rules.plain_english: Apart from the downpayment, a home improvement contractor may not ask for or take any payment that is more than the value of the work actually done or materials actually delivered. This also applies to advance payments from a lender or financing company.
rules.applies_to: Home improvement contractors (general or specialty), their agents and salespersons
rules.source_location: PDF page 410 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book
rules.verbatim_quote: (5) Except for a downpayment, the contractor shall neither request nor accept payment that exceeds the value of the work performed or material delivered. The prohibition prescribed by this paragraph extends to advance payment in whole or in part from any lender or financier for the performance or sale of home improvement goods or services.
rules.notes: For a pay-app tool: block any HIC billing line where billed-to-date exceeds percent complete x scheduled value, and do not bill AIA-style 'materials presently stored' unless the material has been delivered (interpretation: stored off-site material is not 'delivered'). CSLB's Nov 3, 2026 Legislative Committee packet lists 'unlawful payment provisions that require payments that exceed value of work performed' and up-front lender payments as key current enforcement concerns.

rules.title: HIC downpayment: lesser of $1,000 or 10% of contract price
rules.plain_english: A home improvement downpayment can be no more than $1,000 or 10% of the contract price, whichever is less, and the contract must show it under a 'Downpayment' heading with the required bold statement.

parameters.heading: Downpayment
parameters.required_statement_text: THE DOWNPAYMENT MAY NOT EXCEED $1,000 OR 10 PERCENT OF THE CONTRACT PRICE, WHICHEVER IS LESS.

rules.source_location: PDF page 410 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book; PDF page 400 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book
rules.verbatim_quote: (3) If a downpayment will be charged, the downpayment shall not exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) or 10 percent of the contract amount, whichever amount is less.
rules.notes: Violation of 7159.5(a)(3) is a misdemeanor (7159.5(b)(1)). Swimming pool contracts have their own rules (B&P 7167) not covered here.

rules.title: HIC contract price in dollars and cents, all-in; finance charge separate
rules.plain_english: The home improvement contract must state the agreed price in dollars and cents under the heading 'Contract Price', and that price must include everything (profit, labor, materials). Any finance charge must be shown separately under 'Finance Charge'.

rules.notes: Original contract sum on a pay application (G702 line 1) for an HIC should equal this figure. 7159.5(a)(2): a separate finance charge 'shall be set out separately from the contract amount.'

rules.title: HIC progress payments must add up to contract price minus downpayment
rules.plain_english: CSLB's worksheet: take the total contract price, subtract the downpayment, and the sum of all progress payments in the schedule should equal what is left. Each payment is due when its phase of work is complete.

rules.title: Allowance overruns/underruns change the price only by written change order
rules.plain_english: If the contract price includes allowances for items not yet selected, and the final cost is more or less than the allowance, the contract price goes up or down through a written change order. CSLB's sample says allowances include overhead, profit and sales tax.
rules.applies_to: Home improvement contracts using allowances (good practice for any contract)

rules.title: Bonded/joint-control HIC contractors exempt from downpayment and progress-payment limits
rules.plain_english: A home improvement contractor that furnishes a full performance and payment bond, lien and completion bond, registrar-approved bond equivalent, or joint control covering full performance and payment is exempt from the downpayment cap, the schedule-of-payments rule and the no-payment-ahead-of-work rule, and may take payment before completion.

rules.title: HIC salesperson commission paid pro rata with contractor's payments
rules.plain_english: If a salesperson's commission comes out of the contract price, it must be paid out in proportion to the payments the contractor actually receives under the payment schedule, not up front.

rules.title: HIC payment violations are misdemeanors ($100-$5,000 fine, up to 1 year jail)
rules.plain_english: Violating the written-contract/price rule, the downpayment cap, or the no-payment-ahead-of-work rule on a home improvement job is a misdemeanor: a fine of $100 to $5,000, up to a year in county jail, or both. In a declared disaster area the court must impose the maximum fine.

rules.title: Schedule of values / continuation sheet (G703-style) math
rules.plain_english: Break the contract sum into line items whose scheduled values add up exactly to the contract sum. Each period, for every line: work completed to date = previous + this period + materials presently stored; percent complete = completed to date / scheduled value; balance to finish = scheduled value - completed to date; retainage = retention rate x completed to date (or per line if rates vary).

columns.D: work completed from previous application (D+E of prior app)
columns.F: materials presently stored (not in D or E)
columns.G: total completed and stored to date = D + E + F

checks: G <= C for each line (no overbilling a line)
change orders added as new SOV lines or adjusted lines when approved
ca_overlays: HIC: no billing beyond work performed/material delivered (B&P 7159.5(a)(5))
retention caps: private 5% for contracts on/after 2026-01-01 (Civ. Code 8811), public 5% (PCC 7201)

rules.title: Application for payment (G702-style) summary math
rules.plain_english: The pay application summary rolls up the SOV: original contract sum + net change orders = contract sum to date; total completed and stored to date minus retainage = total earned less retainage; subtract previous certificates for payment to get the current payment due; balance to finish including retainage = contract sum to date - total earned less retainage.

lines.2: net change by change orders (approved only)
lines.4: total completed and stored to date (sum of SOV column G)
lines.5a: retainage on completed work = rate x (D+E)
lines.5b: retainage on stored material = rate x F
lines.7: less previous certificates for payment (line 6 of prior certificate)

rules.title: Percentage-of-completion revenue; costs vs. billings (WIP)
rules.plain_english: On long jobs, revenue and profit can be recognized by percent complete (e.g., 50% done = 50% of estimated revenue and profit earned). Comparing earned revenue with amounts billed shows over-billing (billings in excess of costs/earnings) or under-billing (costs in excess of billings).

parameters.under_billing: earned_revenue - billings_to_date (if positive; 'costs in excess of billings')
parameters.alternative_method: completed contract method (recognize all at completion)

rules.applies_to: Contractors' job-cost accounting and WIP schedules

For example, if the work performed each year is estimated to represent 50 percent of total performance under contract, then 50 percent of the total estimated revenue and profit is considered earned.
rules.notes: Quote is from the CSLB Law Book's non-binding business-management guidance chapter (official publication, but guidance, not law), so it is marked as a practice item. rules.title: Retention defined (Law Book still says 'usually 10 percent' - outdated for new private contracts)
rules.plain_english: Retention is money held back from each progress payment until the job is completed and accepted; it is earned but unpaid. The Law Book says 'usually 10 percent', but private contracts entered on or after January 1, 2026 are capped at 5% (with exceptions) and public works are capped at 5%.
rules.citation: CSLB Law Book Ch. 3 guidance; Civil Code 8811 (SB 61, Stats 2025 ch 49); PCC 7201
rules.source_location: PDF page 54 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book; PDF page 61 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book
rules.verbatim_quote: Retention: A specified amount, usually 10 percent, withheld from progress payments to the contractor pending satisfactory completion and final acceptance of the project. You have already earned this amount even though you have not yet been paid.
rules.notes: Quote is from the CSLB Law Book's non-binding business-management guidance chapter (official publication, but guidance, not law), so it is marked as a practice item. CONFLICT: the 2026 Law Book's business chapter (PDF pages 54, 61-62) still describes 10% retention and 'the final 10 percent upon completion and expiration of the lien period'. Do not default a calculator to 10% for private contracts entered on/after 2026-01-01 unless an SB 61 exemption applies (see private-retention-5pct-cap and private-retention-cap-exemptions).

rules.title: Private works retention capped at 5% (contracts entered on/after 1/1/2026)
rules.plain_english: On private jobs under contracts signed on or after January 1, 2026, retention held from any payment (owner to GC, GC to sub, sub to sub-tier) cannot exceed 5% of the payment, total retention cannot exceed 5% of the contract price, and a subcontract cannot use a higher retention percentage than the owner-GC contract. The winner of a lawsuit to enforce this gets attorney's fees.

rules.title: Retention math on each pay application
rules.plain_english: Compute retention each period as the retention rate times the work completed (and stored materials, if retained) this period, stop when the total hits the contract cap, and release it at completion after deducting no more than the legally allowed amount for genuine disputes.

rules.title: Public works retention capped at 5%
rules.plain_english: On California public works contracts (entered on or after 2012-01-01), retention may not exceed 5% of any payment or 5% of the contract price in total, and subcontract retention may not exceed the prime-contract percentage. Exceptions: (a) a subcontractor that was told in writing before or at the bid request that bonds are required and then cannot or will not furnish an admitted-surety performance and payment bond; (b) a project the agency found "substantially complex" before bid, with the basis and actual retention stated in the bid documents (local agencies: finding approved at a noticed public hearing). No party may require a waiver.

parameters.exception: pre-bid finding that the project is substantially complex, with basis and actual retention amount stated in bid documents (local agencies: finding approved project-by-project at a properly noticed, normally scheduled public hearing)
parameters.exception_sub_bond_failure: contractor gave written notice (PCC 4108(c)) before or at bid request that bonds are required, and subcontractor is unable or refuses to furnish an admitted-surety performance and payment bond
parameters.does_not_limit: withholding 150% of disputed amounts from final payment under PCC 7107(c)

rules.title: HIC change orders must be in writing and signed before the changed work starts
rules.plain_english: On a home improvement job, the contract must incorporate a change-order form, and a change becomes part of the contract only if it is written and signed by both parties before any of the changed or extra work begins.

rules.title: LLC licensees: liability insurance $1M aggregate (+$100k per person over 5, max $5M)

rules.title: CSLB arbitration: mandatory at or below $25,000 (contract price or damages); voluntary above $25,000 and under $50,000
rules.plain_english: CSLB must refer an eligible complaint to its free arbitration program, without the parties' consent, when the contract price or the damages demanded is $25,000 (the license bond amount) or less. rules.title: Small claims: money judgments up to $12,500 (no lien foreclosure)
rules.plain_english: A contractor owed money can sue in small claims court for up to $12,500 if it is a natural person or sole proprietor; a corporation, partnership, LLC or other entity is limited to $6,250.
